[Think]
Monetarist lens: compare M2 growth (5.4%) with trend real growth (~2%) plus the 3.5-4.5% inflation band, and note nominal GDP at 5.5% against money growth of 5.4%, implying velocity growth near zero. A Chinese developer default on offshore bonds is a credit-market event with limited direct effect on US money supply; it operates through risk aversion, which raises money demand and lowers velocity in the short run, as the framework describes. Money growth is decelerating and nominal GDP is running slightly above it, so the regime is one of money roughly matched to spending with inflation still above the band on core measures. Monetarism treats such a shock as a demand-side financial disturbance that matters only if money quantity is altered; with the Fed's rule-based path unchanged, the event is largely transmitted through spreads and sentiment rather than through the money stock.

[Output]
Causal chain: Chinese developer default -> offshore EM/Asia credit repricing and rising global risk aversion (VIX, high-yield spreads widen) -> higher precautionary money demand and lower velocity in the short run -> money growth does not accelerate, so no change in the quantity relative to demand -> modest drag on US nominal spending and some disinflationary pressure -> outcome: slight growth softening, inflation drifting toward target without a monetary-driven collapse.

Scenarios:
S1 (contained default, risk aversion fades; growth flat, inflation down): 0.62
S2 (wider credit contagion via high-yield and offshore funding; growth down, inflation down): 0.28
S3 (liquidity-driven rebound with money growth accelerating above trend-plus-target; growth up, inflation up): 0.10

Signals:
equities: NEUTRAL (2) - nominal spending near trend offers no clear monetary tailwind; sentiment shock is offset by unchanged money growth.
government bonds: LONG (3) - the flight-to-quality rise in money demand and falling velocity point to lower yields as inflation eases toward band.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (2) - no change in relative money growth between the US and the rest of the world to justify a directional view.
gold: NEUTRAL (2) - real rates and money growth are not moving enough to set a clear monetary direction.
oil: NEUTRAL (3) - no supply shock and no money accommodation signal; oil moves with money-driven demand, which is flat.
credit: SHORT (3) - high-yield spreads at 460bp leave room to widen as risk aversion rises and funding conditions tighten.

[Think]
Within the monetarist frame, the key diagnostic is money growth against trend real growth plus the inflation target. US M2 growth is 11.9% y/y, down from 13.2%, but still far above the roughly 2% trend real growth plus the 3.5-4.5% inflation band (about 5.5-6.5% total), so money is running well ahead of the consistent rate and is the source of excess nominal demand. Nominal GDP at 6.6% sits near the top of that consistent range, and implied velocity growth is nominal GDP minus money growth, about -5.3%, showing money being held rather than spent as rates rose. The sanctions shock is a supply shock, so the framework says it becomes persistent inflation only if money accommodates it; with M2 decelerating and velocity falling, accommodation is not evident in the data, but the excess level of money means the risk is not absent. Long and variable lags mean the policy stance feeds through slowly, and the rule-based response is to hold money growth steady rather than validate the oil-driven price level.

[Output]
Causal chain: sanctions on a major oil exporter -> crude supply tightens (WTI already near $97) -> headline energy prices rise, raising CPI above the target band -> monetarist test: money growth does not accommodate (M2 decelerating, velocity falling) -> relative-price shock stays a one-off level shift rather than persistent inflation -> real incomes squeezed, growth softens while the rule-based stance holds -> outcome: temporary higher headline inflation, with core inflation contained if expectations stay anchored.

Scenarios:
S1 (Contained supply shock, money does not accommodate; growth down, inflation up): 0.50
S2 (Stagflationary spiral, money accommodates the shock; growth down, inflation up): 0.25
S3 (Oil shock fades quickly, disinflation continues; growth flat, inflation down): 0.25

Signals:
equities: SHORT (conviction 2) - energy-cost squeeze on margins and real incomes as growth slows, with the rule-based path limiting the damage.
government bonds: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - supply-driven inflation argues for higher yields, but a credible rule-based stance and falling velocity cap the term-premium rise.
US dollar: LONG (conviction 2) - relative policy credibility and a US energy position support the dollar against the sanctions backdrop.
gold: NEUTRAL (conviction 1) - no monetary-regime shift is signalled, so the metal has no clear monetarist driver.
oil: LONG (conviction 3) - the sanctioned supply loss directly tightens the market, and the price move is the event's first-order effect.
credit: SHORT (conviction 3) - the high-yield spread at 760bp already embeds stress, and slower nominal growth widens it further.

[Think]
Monetarist diagnosis: M2 growth has slowed from 7.7% to 5.5%, and nominal GDP growth is also 5.5%, so implied velocity growth is roughly zero, a sign money is being spent at a steady pace rather than hoarded. Real trend growth of about 2% plus the 3.5-4.5% inflation band implies a steady-state money growth of roughly 5.5-6.5%, so current M2 growth sits near the consistent range and is not an accelerating impulse. The -1.0% four-quarter average is cyclical, not trend, and the -3.4% quarterly print is a transient contraction that does not alter the trend read. The banking event is a deposit-guarantee measure: it protects the money stock from a run-driven collapse in deposits, which is precisely the failure mode the monetarist framework warns about, since a fall in broad money would transmit into spending and prices with long and variable lags. Guaranteeing deposits keeps M2 from contracting and keeps money growth anchored, consistent with a credible rule-based stance.

[Output]
Causal chain: bank failures and deposit-flight risk -> regulators guarantee all deposits -> deposits (and M2) are protected from a forced contraction -> money growth stays near trend-consistent rates, velocity stable -> nominal spending does not collapse -> inflation drifts toward the band as the earlier monetary deceleration works through with long lags, while the growth shortfall is treated as cyclical -> disinflation without a broad money or velocity collapse.

Scenarios:
S1 (deposit guarantee contains the run; M2 stable, disinflation continues without a spending collapse; growth flat-to-up, inflation down): 0.55
S2 (lagged effect of the earlier M2 slowdown deepens the contraction despite the guarantee; growth down, inflation down): 0.25
S3 (guarantee revives money and credit creation too strongly; growth up, inflation up): 0.20

Signals:
equities: LONG (conviction 3) - contained banking stress and money growth near trend-consistent levels support a recovery in nominal spending and earnings.
government bonds: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - disinflation argues for lower long yields, but the 262bp curve and stable money growth limit the case for a strong directional view.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - no clear monetary-growth differential against major peers from the information given.
gold: SHORT (conviction 2) - no monetary debasement signal: M2 growth is slowing toward trend and velocity is steady, reducing the case for a hedge bid.
oil: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - a $99 price is a relative-price shock; under this framework it becomes inflation only if money accommodates it, and money growth is not accelerating.
credit: LONG (conviction 3) - guaranteed deposits reduce the risk of forced deleveraging, supporting spreads that have room to narrow from 743bp.

[Think]
Monetarist diagnosis: M2 growth is 6.4% against trend real growth of about 2% plus a 4% inflation target, so money growth sits well above what the economy needs. Yet nominal GDP is -2.1% y/y, which implies velocity growth of roughly -8.5%, a sharp collapse consistent with money being hoarded as demand for it surges. A GDP beat from a -5.5% annualised quarter reflects the cycle (4-quarter average -1.7%), not trend, so it does not by itself change the monetary picture. Money held as precautionary balances will only reach spending when quantity outruns demand, and with velocity falling this sharply the excess money is likely to stay idle for now, with long and variable lags governing when it re-enters. The rebound is a cyclical bounce from a depressed base rather than evidence of a rule-based shift in policy.

[Output]
Causal chain: GDP beats consensus -> cyclical rebound in measured nominal and real output off a depressed base -> implied velocity decline narrows as nominal GDP recovers from -2.1% y/y -> excess M2 (6.4% vs roughly 6% needed) begins to reach spending as money demand stabilises -> inflation expectations firm toward the target band -> gradual normalisation, with outcome contingent on lags and on whether velocity keeps falling.

Scenarios:
S1 (cyclical rebound, velocity stabilises: growth up, inflation up): 0.45
S2 (idle money persists, velocity keeps falling: growth flat, inflation flat): 0.35
S3 (excess money overshoots into spending, expectations unanchor: growth up, inflation up sharply): 0.20

Signals:
equities: LONG (3) - nominal recovery and a rebound in output favour cyclical earnings as velocity stabilises.
government bonds: SHORT (2) - firmer nominal growth and expectations toward the target lift yields from a 1.06% 10y base.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (2) - monetary growth well above trend argues against strength, offset by the rebound in relative growth.
gold: NEUTRAL (2) - excess money supports the store of value case, but falling velocity and a near-term recovery offset it.
oil: NEUTRAL (2) - WTI at $35 gives little signal from the monetary side; demand recovery is supportive, supply is not in view.
credit: LONG (3) - a 650bp high-yield spread prices in stress that a cyclical rebound and stable money growth should compress.

[Think]
Monetarist lens: nominal GDP growth is 4.0% against money (M2) growth of 2.0%, implying velocity growth of roughly +2.0%, which is a rise in velocity, consistent with money being held less tightly than demand requires and with inflation running above the target band on core measures (core PCE 3.2%, CPI 2.7%). Real growth trend is about 2%; the 4-quarter average of 1.3% reflects the cycle, not the trend, so output is somewhat below potential. A 15% across-the-board tariff is a relative-price shock to tradables, and under this framework it becomes sustained inflation only if money growth accommodates it; with M2 at 2.0% and only recently recovering from -0.1%, money growth does not visibly accommodate, so the expected effect is a one-off level shift in prices and a drag on real activity, not a lasting rise in the inflation rate. Long and variable lags mean any real-activity damage from the tariff shows up with delay, while the price-level effect is front-loaded.

[Output]
Causal chain: tariff announcement -> higher import prices and reduced import volumes (relative-price shock to tradables) -> one-off upward step in the price level, partly offset by weaker real demand and a modest squeeze on profit margins -> with M2 growth not accommodating, no sustained rise in nominal spending growth -> inflation drifts up temporarily then fades toward the 3.5-4.5% band as the level effect passes through, while real output growth slows toward and below trend over the subsequent year.

Scenarios:
S1 (tariff level shift absorbed, money growth unaccommodating; growth down modestly, inflation up temporarily then fading): 0.55
S2 (tariff triggers retaliation and sharper trade contraction; growth down, inflation up): 0.25
S3 (tariff effect contained, trade diversion, growth flat, inflation flat): 0.20

Signals:
equities: SHORT (2) - tariff-exposed import-dependent margins face a real-income and cost squeeze as the level shift hits before money growth supports nominal revenues.
government bonds: NEUTRAL (2) - a one-off price level effect and weaker real activity pull yields in opposite directions, and the monetarist view gives no clear lasting inflation signal.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (2) - tariffs weaken import demand for foreign currency but the monetarist framework ties the currency to relative money growth, which gives no decisive reading.
gold: NEUTRAL (1) - no sustained change in money growth means no monetary-debasement trigger.
oil: NEUTRAL (2) - tariffs on energy-intensive inputs raise costs, but without money accommodation the effect is a one-off level shift rather than a sustained price trend.
credit: SHORT (2) - high-yield spreads at 552bp are vulnerable to weaker real growth and margin pressure from tariffs, with the 2% M2 growth offering little support.

[Think]
The output gap is roughly neutral-to-slightly-overheated on the data given: unemployment at 3.8% sits below the 4.5% natural rate, and inflation runs well above the 2% target (CPI 3.0%, core PCE 3.7%), so the US is in a positive gap with restraint, not support, as the appropriate stance. Real GDP at 2.5% four-quarter average exceeds trend-consistent growth, consistent with demand running ahead of supply. A Chinese developer default is a shock to Chinese demand and to global credit confidence, which in Keynesian terms transmits through lower confidence and investment (animal spirits) and weaker export demand for US goods, a negative demand impulse. Given the positive US gap, that demand shortfall is mildly welcome as a cooling force rather than a recessionary threat. Sticky prices mean the inflation effect of a demand dip arrives slowly, so the near-term result is softer growth with inflation still elevated.

[Output]
Causal chain: Chinese developer default -> weaker Chinese property investment and household confidence -> lower Chinese import demand and higher global risk aversion (HY spread and VIX widen modestly) -> reduced external demand and tighter financial conditions for US firms -> US aggregate demand eases from an overheated level -> output gap narrows, unemployment drifts up slightly, core inflation eases only gradually given sticky prices and wages -> outcome: softer US growth with inflation still above target, Fed keeps policy restrictive, yields fall modestly at the front end.

Scenarios:
S1 (contained cooling, Chinese shock stays regional; growth down, inflation down): 0.50
S2 (global confidence hit with tighter credit; growth down, inflation down sharply): 0.30
S3 (shock offset by Chinese stimulus and steady US demand; growth flat, inflation flat): 0.20

Signals:
equities: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - softer demand helps cool the overheated economy but earnings risk from weaker global demand offsets it.
government bonds: LONG (conviction 3) - a narrowing positive output gap and easing demand pressure lower the expected path of policy rates, supporting Treasuries.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - safe-haven demand supports the dollar while lower US rate expectations weigh on it.
gold: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - falling real rates support gold, but the shock is not severe enough to drive a strong stress bid.
oil: SHORT (conviction 3) - weaker Chinese and global demand reduces oil consumption, pressuring WTI from $55.
credit: SHORT (conviction 3) - high-yield spreads at 460bp are vulnerable to widening as global risk appetite deteriorates.

[Think]
Using the Keynesian output-gap lens: unemployment at 5.3% against a 4.5% natural rate implies a negative unemployment gap of roughly 0.8 points, which by the rule of thumb (output gap moves about twice the unemployment gap) is a sizeable negative output gap of around 1.6% of potential. Inflation at 5.0% CPI and 3.9% core PCE is well above the 2% target, so the economy simultaneously shows slack in labour and excess price pressure, pointing to a supply-driven inflation problem layered on weak demand. A sanctions shock on a major oil exporter is a negative supply shock: the price effect (WTI at $97 rising further) raises headline inflation, while the income effect transfers purchasing power from oil consumers to producers and squeezes real demand, which in a economy already running a negative gap likely dominates the policy read. Sticky wages and prices mean the adjustment falls mainly on output and employment rather than prices. Rates sit at 4.75%, well above zero, so no liquidity trap constrains policy, and fiscal or monetary support remains available to close the negative gap, though inflation above target limits how far easing can go.

[Output]
Causal chain: sanctions on major oil exporter -> crude supply tightens and oil rises further -> headline and energy-driven inflation pressure lifts price level -> real incomes squeezed and consumer demand weakens while the output gap is already negative -> growth slows further and unemployment drifts up -> policy faces stagflationary trade-off; central bank holds or eases cautiously, with fiscal support favoured to restore demand -> risk-off sentiment (VIX 32, high-yield spread 760bp) widens credit spreads and supports safe-haven demand.

Scenarios:
S1 (oil-supply squeeze with demand drag: growth down, inflation up): 0.50
S2 (contained shock, fiscal/monetary support closes gap: growth flat, inflation flat): 0.30
S3 (sharp stagflation and recession, growth down, inflation down as demand collapses): 0.20

Signals:
equities: SHORT (3) - negative output gap plus income squeeze from higher energy costs weighs on earnings and demand; partial offset if support is announced.
government bonds: LONG (3) - weaker demand and rising recession risk pull yields down and support safe-haven demand, though above-target inflation caps the rally.
US dollar: LONG (2) - stress and safe-haven flows favour the dollar relative to the baseline, with US energy self-sufficiency a modest support.
gold: LONG (3) - real rates falling on demand weakness and geopolitical stress support gold as a hedge.
oil: LONG (4) - direct supply shock from sanctions on a major exporter pushes prices higher from an already elevated $97.
credit: SHORT (4) - high-yield spreads at 760bp widen further as growth slows and defaults rise.

[Think]
Using the Keynesian lens, the output gap is the first read. Unemployment at 5.4% sits about 0.9 points above the 4.5% natural rate, a positive unemployment gap, while core PCE at 5.5% is far above the 2% target. Output growth is contracting (-3.4% q/q saar; -1.0% four-quarter average), so demand is weakening even though the labour market has not yet broken, which points to a tightening-induced slowdown rather than a clear negative gap. The policy rate of 1.75% is far from the zero bound, so a liquidity trap is not the operative constraint; monetary space exists but inflation argues against easing. A deposit guarantee is a narrow financial backstop: it protects deposit balances and limits a run that would otherwise drive a credit collapse and a sharp fall in aggregate demand, which is the channel Keynesians care about. The oil price of $99 is an income transfer from consumers and a cost shock, and with core inflation this high, the price effect is likely to dominate in the near term, keeping restraint in play. The guarantee therefore reduces the tail of a demand collapse without signalling a change in the inflation-fighting stance.

[Output]
Causal chain: bank failures and deposit runs -> guarantee of deposits limits the run and stabilises bank funding -> credit supply and confidence do not collapse, so private demand falls less sharply than in an unguarded panic -> output contraction is contained, but tight policy and sticky inflation persist -> growth weakens modestly, inflation eases only slowly, and the tightening cycle is at risk of ending earlier.

Scenarios:
S1 (guarantee contains the run, policy holds; growth flat, inflation flat): 0.45
S2 (credit tightening deepens the slowdown, forcing an early pause; growth down, inflation down): 0.35
S3 (guarantee plus easing expectations revive demand while core inflation stays sticky; growth up, inflation up): 0.20

equities: SHORT (3) - a demand slowdown and higher risk premia from a tighter credit channel weigh on earnings, though the guarantee caps the downside.
government bonds: LONG (3) - a shift toward pausing restraint and rising recession risk pulls front-end yields down, steepening the curve from its inverted level.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (2) - safe-haven demand offsets the prospect of a slower policy path; no clear directional edge.
gold: LONG (3) - falling real rates and financial stress support gold as yields on the front end fall.
oil: SHORT (2) - slowing demand from a credit-driven contraction weakens the outlook for crude, though the level of $99 remains supported by supply.
credit: SHORT (3) - high-yield spreads at 743bp are vulnerable to widening as default risk rises in a contracting economy, even with deposit protection.

[Think]
The data show a deep negative output gap: unemployment at 5.7% against a natural rate near 4.5% is a gap of roughly 1.2 points, which by the rule of thumb (output gap about twice the unemployment gap) implies output sitting around 2.4% below potential. Inflation is well below the 2% target (CPI -0.4%, core PCE 1.0%), and the policy rate at 0.125% sits at the zero bound, so we are in a liquidity trap where conventional easing has little room. Nominal GDP growth of -2.1% and a four-quarter real average of -1.7% confirm demand shortfall as the dominant risk. A GDP beat from a -5.5% annualised base is therefore good news in this framework: it signals demand recovery and narrows a negative gap, which is the direction support is meant to push the economy. Because the gap is negative, the beat does not yet threaten overheating, so it reduces the need for future restraint rather than raising near-term rate expectations.

[Output]
Causal chain: GDP beats consensus -> evidence that aggregate demand is recovering from a deep negative output gap -> higher expected income and sales lift business and household confidence (animal spirits) -> investment and hiring firm up, unemployment drifts down toward the natural rate -> inflation expectations improve from very low levels while the gap is still negative, so real rates fall and the recovery is not choked off -> outcome: a narrower output gap, a better growth path, and reduced tail risk of prolonged demand-deficient stagnation.

Scenarios:
S1 (demand recovery narrows gap; growth up, inflation up): 0.55
S2 (beat proves a one-off rebound, gap stays wide; growth flat, inflation flat): 0.33
S3 (liquidity trap persists, demand relapses; growth down, inflation down): 0.12

Signals:
equities: LONG (4) - demand recovery and rising earnings expectations from a negative output gap favour cyclical equities.
government bonds: SHORT (2) - stronger growth lifts term premia and yields modestly, though the zero bound limits the move at the front end.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (2) - faster recovery supports the currency, offset by the still-large gap and near-zero policy rate keeping relative rate advantage limited.
gold: NEUTRAL (2) - falling real rates from better growth are offset by reduced safe-haven demand as stress eases.
oil: LONG (3) - a demand-led recovery from a $35 base raises energy consumption and supports prices.
credit: LONG (3) - the high-yield spread of 650bp is wide relative to a narrowing output gap, so spreads should compress as default risk falls.

[Think]
Unemployment at 4.0% sits below the 4.5% natural rate, and core PCE at 3.2% is above the 2% target, so the output gap is positive: the economy is running hot, not slack. Real GDP at 1.5% q/q saar and 1.3% over four quarters is near trend, with no sign of demand collapse that would call for support. A 15% across-the-board tariff is a supply shock to import prices, so its price effect (higher import costs feeding core goods inflation) pushes inflation up, while the income effect (a transfer from households and firms to the tariff revenue base and reduced real purchasing power) weakens demand. With the economy already overheated, the price effect dominates in the policy-relevant sense: it raises inflation above target and gives the central bank no reason to ease, so the likely reaction is restraint or at least no cut. The paradox of thrift is not central here, and the policy rate at 0.125% is not the binding issue because the gap is positive, not negative. Confidence effects from trade escalation are negative for investment, which in a hot economy is a modest drag rather than a recession trigger.

[Output]
Causal chain: 15% tariff -> higher landed import prices -> core goods inflation rises above the already-elevated 3.2% core PCE -> inflation further above 2% target while unemployment sits below natural rate -> central bank holds or signals restraint rather than easing -> real rates stay firm, higher-for-longer curve -> demand softened by lower real incomes and weaker business investment confidence -> growth slows toward or below trend, unemployment drifts up only slowly from 4.0%.

Scenarios:
S1 (tariff inflation pass-through with restraint; growth down, inflation up): 0.50
S2 (tariff drag with contained pass-through; growth flat, inflation flat): 0.35
S3 (trade-war escalation and confidence shock tipping to contraction; growth down, inflation down): 0.15

Signals:
equities: SHORT (conviction 2) - higher real rates and margin squeeze from imported input costs in a positive-gap economy outweigh any relief.
government bonds: SHORT (conviction 3) - inflation above target and no easing bias push the curve up, consistent with restraint; a flight-to-quality bid is a weaker offset given the gap is positive.
US dollar: LONG (conviction 2) - firmer real rates and relative restraint support the dollar against a backdrop of trade-driven uncertainty.
gold: SHORT (conviction 2) - it tracks real rates, which are rising with restraint; stress-driven demand is secondary when the economy is overheating rather than in slump.
oil: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - a tariff is not a direct energy supply shock, and the demand drag from slower growth roughly offsets any cost pass-through.
credit: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - a high-yield spread of 552bp reflects some risk premium, but with growth near trend and no recession signal, the tariff effect on defaults is gradual rather than immediate.

[Think]
The default of a large Chinese property developer on offshore bonds is a liquidation event, but the Austrian question is whether it removes or adds intervention and distortion. Here the data show a US policy rate of 2.5% against CPI of 3.0%, giving a real policy rate of about -0.5%, well below the roughly 2% natural rate; that is artificially cheap credit, and M2 growth of 5.4% with nominal GDP at 5.5% confirms money is being created. Credit has therefore been distorted for a while, so the Chinese default is the visible end of a malinvestment cycle built on cheap dollar and yuan credit, and its correction is healthy in principle. The short-run pain falls on creditors and on the developer's own capital structure, and the framework judges that pain as the necessary liquidation rather than as a reason for stimulus. Whether it spreads to the US depends on how much offshore Chinese property paper is held by US and global lenders, and on whether authorities bail it out, which would add intervention rather than remove it.

[Output]
Causal chain: Chinese developer defaults on offshore bonds -> losses crystallise on malinvested property capital and force writedowns on leveraged holders of Chinese credit -> risk premia widen for offshore Asian and EM high-yield paper -> capital is reallocated away from the misallocated sector toward sounder uses, while the US high-yield spread of 460bp reprices modestly -> US growth slows somewhat from a still-positive trend, with the 2.5% policy rate exposing the underlying real-rate distortion, and any recovery rests on genuine saving rather than new money creation.

Scenarios:
S1 (contained liquidation, no bailout; growth flat, inflation down): 0.50
S2 (spillover into global credit and risk-off; growth down, inflation down): 0.35
S3 (bailout and renewed easing that re-inflates the distortion; growth up, inflation up): 0.15

equities: SHORT (conviction 2) - a credit-spread widening and reduced global risk appetite pressure equity multiples, especially in leveraged sectors exposed to Chinese demand.
government bonds: LONG (conviction 2) - deflationary risk-off demand and eventual rate normalisation pulling real yields down support Treasuries despite the 13bp curve slope.
US dollar: LONG (conviction 2) - flight to dollar liquidity during offshore Chinese credit stress outweighs the 104 DXY level already elevated.
gold: SHORT (conviction 3) - gold gains when real rates are negative and money is being created, but a liquidation that clears without a bailout lifts real yields and removes that support.
oil: SHORT (conviction 2) - weaker Chinese property demand and slower global growth reduce industrial and energy consumption from the $55 WTI base.
credit: SHORT (conviction 4) - the 460bp US high-yield spread and offshore Chinese paper are most exposed to repricing as malinvestment is written down.

[Think]
Broad sanctions on a major oil exporter are a supply-side restriction layered onto a system already carrying distorted credit. The data show policy rate 4.75 against CPI 5.0, so the real policy rate is roughly -0.25%, well below the ~2% natural rate; credit is artificially cheap and M2 growth of 11.9% signals continued money creation. Sanctions add a further price distortion (oil at $97) rather than removing one, which the framework reads as adding malinvestment pressure rather than clearing it. The yield curve is still positive (46bp), so this is not yet a fully mature bust signal, and high-yield spreads at 760bp show some credit stress but not a broad liquidation. Because the event is inflationary and the real rate is negative, hard assets have the favourable setup, while financial assets dependent on cheap credit face the risk that the price distortion eventually forces a rate response that ends the boom.

[Output]
Causal chain: sanctions remove oil supply -> energy prices rise further on top of already-high inflation -> real policy rate deepens its negative gap, or the central bank is pressed into a tightening that exposes leveraged malinvestment -> credit spreads widen and real activity slows -> the boom-bust is either delayed by continued money creation (stagflationary drift) or forced into liquidation (bust).

Scenarios:
S1 (Stagflationary drift under money creation; growth down, inflation up): 0.45
S2 (Forced tightening and credit liquidation; growth down, inflation down): 0.30
S3 (Contained shock, supply absorbed without a policy response; growth flat, inflation up): 0.25

Signals:
equities: SHORT (conviction 3) - credit-dependent valuations and margin pressure from energy costs; the malinvestment built on cheap money is exposed as real rates stay negative and growth slows.
government bonds: SHORT (conviction 3) - inflation pressure and money creation erode real returns while term premium rises on the stagflation risk.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - a safe-haven bid competes with the relative tightening outlook and the dollar's role in dollar-priced oil; no clear directional edge.
gold: LONG (conviction 4) - hard asset with negative real rates, rising M2 and sanctions-driven geopolitical hedging demand.
oil: LONG (conviction 4) - sanctions remove supply from a major exporter into a market already priced at $97, so the price distortion persists or widens.
credit: SHORT (conviction 3) - high-yield spreads at 760bp are vulnerable to widening if the tightening or liquidation scenario unfolds, and cheap credit is the source of the imbalance.

[Think]
The event is a deposit guarantee at failed banks, which adds state backing to liabilities and so extends implicit intervention: it socialises losses and blunts the market's signal that unsound banks should fail. Judged by the framework's test, this adds intervention rather than removing it. The credit backdrop is also telling: the policy rate of 1.75% sits well below 6.5% CPI, a real policy rate near -4.75%, far below the ~2% natural rate, and M2 growth of 5.5% on a 7.7% prior year still reflects a monetary expansion that was artificially cheap. Those data show a credit boom having been fed by negative real rates, which is what the liquidation needs. The guarantee therefore postpones the necessary liquidation of the malinvestment that such cheap credit produced, keeping the structure of production distorted. Hard assets look favoured while real rates are negative and money is still expanding, while the deflationary bust is being deferred rather than avoided.

[Output]
Causal chain: deposit guarantees at failed banks -> reduced market discipline and bailout expectations spread to other banks -> bank losses socialised, the malinvestment from cheap credit (real policy rate ~-4.75%, M2 still growing) is not liquidated -> distorted production structure persists and time preference is pushed toward consumption -> monetary and credit support needed to keep the system intact sustains inflationary pressure, and the eventual correction is larger and later.

Scenarios:
S1 (guarantee-led postponement, bust deferred; growth flat-to-down, inflation up): 0.45
S2 (clean liquidation after limited intervention, deflationary correction; growth down, inflation down): 0.35
S3 (stagflationary squeeze as money keeps expanding under oil and inflation pressure; growth down, inflation up): 0.20

Signals:
equities: SHORT (conviction 3) - malinvestment built on cheap credit is unwound with earnings pressure as real rates stay negative while growth contracts.
government bonds: SHORT (conviction 2) - positive term premium and inflation risk from monetary support outweigh any flight to safety at a 3.79% 10y yield.
US dollar: NEUTRAL (conviction 2) - guaranteed-deposit expansion and money creation weigh on the dollar, offset by its safe-haven status in stress.
